evaluation.positioning_hook: A panic-stricken college student who can’t die or stay in the same timeline becomes the prime suspect in a string of impossible murders, forcing a hard-nosed NYPD detective to believe him before time resets again.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The hook is immediately legible: an impossible-murder mystery with a time-bending protagonist and a detective on his trail. It has a clear genre promise and a strong hook for thriller and fantasy buyers, though the tonal oddness and specificity narrow it from broad four-quadrant play.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The premise lands fast in the cold open with the bus murder, then sharpens when Ji-a realizes Anthony is tied to the case and time is slipping. The script makes the central engine easy to explain in two sentences: a young man is trapped in a repeating, reality-bending murder pattern, and a detective is the only person who can track it.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Anthony’s panic, guilt, and people-pleasing make him sympathetic, and Ji-a’s blunt competence gives the story a strong counterweight. Joan adds warmth and friction, but the page still leans more on premise than on fully differentiated character depth.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script takes a familiar detective chase and folds in time distortion, memory loss, and a surreal, almost deadpan New York texture. The old woman with the Uzi, the clock-eye tattoo, and the repeated resets give it a confident, ownable weirdness.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The opening murder, the evidence disappearance, and the rooftop confrontation create a strong forward pull. The middle spends meaningful time on atmosphere and character banter, which helps voice, but the case progression is still more episodic than escalating.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The script’s core idea feels fresh because the impossible element is embedded in a procedural chase rather than announced as a fantasy premise. Anthony’s repeated near-death resets and Ji-a’s growing awareness create a clean, surprising engine that feels both strange and playable.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The New York bus routes, NYPD process, college campus, and recurring clock imagery create a specific urban texture. The world is still mostly a container for the mystery, but the bus system, evidence board, and time anomalies suggest a larger rule-set underneath.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a distinct off-kilter register: grim murders, casual profanity, deadpan banter, and surreal time mechanics all coexist without feeling random. The Joan/Anthony dialogue especially gives it a lived-in, slightly abrasive comic rhythm that separates it from standard procedural fare.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: There are seeds of deeper mythology in the clock-eye tattoo, the disappearing case file, and the suggestion that Anthony’s condition is bigger than one murder. The page hints at a larger system, but the script is still mostly delivering the surface mystery rather than fully opening the mythology.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Anthony and Joan have the strongest recurring dynamic, and Ji-a/Larry gives the investigation a workable procedural pairing. That said, the script is still lead-driven, with the supporting players functioning more as pressure points than as a true ensemble engine.

lead_characters.name: Anthony Morgan
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late teens to early 20s, college student, likely Black or mixed-race based on the script's social framing and campus context.
lead_characters.hook: A high-achieving, anxious pre-law student who looks like a model citizen until he becomes trapped in a reality where he may have killed someone, may be repeating time, and can’t tell whether he’s a victim, a witness, or a monster. He’s deeply people-pleasing, emotionally frayed, and running on fear, guilt, and instinct.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Jesse Eisenberg in The Social Network or Robert Pattinson in Good Time — a tightly wound, hyper-verbal panic role that lets an actor play intelligence, shame, and escalating unraveling in the same frame.

lead_characters.name: Ji-a Choi
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 30s, NYPD detective, Korean or Korean-American.
lead_characters.hook: A hard-edged detective with a dry, impatient exterior and a real appetite for the truth, even when the truth starts breaking the rules of evidence. She’s the only person in the room who can track the impossible without blinking, and the script gives her a sharp, unsentimental authority.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase lane of Regina King in Watchmen or Carrie Coon in The Leftovers — a controlled, emotionally sealed investigator role that lets an actor project command while slowly revealing vulnerability.

lead_characters.name: Joan
lead_characters.demographics: Female, college-age, student, likely in her early 20s.
lead_characters.hook: Anthony’s closest friend and emotional pressure valve: sharp-tongued, funny, protective, and far more perceptive than she initially lets on. She’s the kind of friend who can make a joke about murder and still land as the most human person in the scene.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Ayo Edebiri in The Bear or Jodie Comer in Killing Eve early heat — fast, funny, emotionally legible dialogue that can pivot from comic relief to real stakes without warning.

lead_characters.name: XII
lead_characters.demographics: Female, ageless/unclear, human-presenting but possibly supernatural or time-displaced.
lead_characters.hook: A swaggering, streetwise enigma who seems to know exactly what Anthony is and what he’s carrying, while treating murder and time manipulation like part of a private joke. She’s the script’s most overt mythology carrier: charming, threatening, and impossible to pin down.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor do what Tilda Swinton did in Suspiria or Cate Blanchett in Nightmare Alley — arrive with instant authority, bend the tone, and make the audience lean in because the character feels bigger than the scene.

lead_characters.name: Larry
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 20s-30s, detective partner / forensic-adjacent police colleague.
lead_characters.hook: A well-meaning, slightly hapless procedural foil who keeps trying to be useful while Ji-a steamrolls him. He gives the investigation a human, comic friction point and helps ground the police side of the story.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of supporting-cop role that gives actors in The Wire or Brooklyn Nine-Nine a steady stream of scene-stealing beats — reactive comedy, procedural utility, and room to build chemistry.

lead_characters.name: Emma
lead_characters.hook: A relationship node in Anthony’s orbit who becomes a casualty of the story’s time distortion and hidden violence. Even in limited page time, she functions as a human cost marker and a clue to Anthony’s social world.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that can do a lot with very little, similar to the emotionally loaded supporting turns in Euphoria or The End of the F***ing World — brief screen time with real narrative consequence.

lead_characters.name: Old Woman
lead_characters.hook: A terrifyingly cheerful assassin whose Uzi ambush in the bus cold open instantly establishes the script’s surreal threat level. She’s less a conventional character than a nightmare trigger, but she’s memorable and scene-defining.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of left-field, high-impact cameo that gives an actor the kind of one-scene notoriety character performers love — think the shocking, scene-stealing energy of a great Fargo or Barry guest turn.

lead_characters.name: Academic Advisor
lead_characters.hook: A calm institutional presence who quietly knows more than she says, especially in the scene where Ji-a’s movement through the room starts to feel wrong. She adds to the script’s creeping sense that reality is slightly off.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a compact, atmospheric role in the vein of prestige-TV institutional characters — the kind of part that lets an actor play stillness, subtext, and unease in a few precise beats.

casting_characteristics: late-teen/early-20s lead with intense internal panic
elderly woman with strong comic-horror timing

notable_requirements: New York street and bus station exteriors
NYPD precinct and evidence board setup

technical.vfx_details: Time-reset effects, disappearing evidence/case continuity, and the visual handling of repeated moments and temporal skips.
technical.sfx_needs: Practical gunfire, blood effects, body hits, and repeated-death staging in the bus cold open.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: genre-forward theatrical or streamer-premiere mystery-thriller with elevated-concept positioning.

budget.note: Contemporary and mostly contained, but the New York exteriors, precinct build, campus coverage, rooftop work, and repeated-time visual effects keep this above a lean indie floor.

casting.note: The lead needs an actor who can play panic, intelligence, and dark comedy without losing sympathy, while Ji-a needs a performer with authority and dry edge; XII is a narrow, high-flavor role.

development.note: The time-bending rules, disappearing evidence, and clock-eye mythology are compelling, but the feature needs a clean internal logic so the mystery payoff feels earned rather than merely strange.

comp_set.title: The Invisible Man
comp_set.why_it_comps: A genre-forward, character-driven thriller built around a protagonist whose reality is doubted while a relentless external threat keeps tightening the vise.

comp_set.title: Happy Death Day
comp_set.why_it_comps: The repeated-death/time-loop mechanics and the blend of horror-adjacent tension with a playable, high-concept engine are a close structural neighbor.

comp_set.title: Source Code
comp_set.why_it_comps: A mystery-thriller where time distortion is the engine, not just the gimmick, and the lead must solve the case while trapped inside the rules.

comp_set.title: The Vast of Night
comp_set.why_it_comps: The script shares its eerie, low-key strangeness and the sense that ordinary spaces are hiding a much larger, stranger system.

audience_target.primary_audience: Viewers who like smart, offbeat mystery-thrillers with a supernatural or time-bending twist and a strong detective-protagonist dynamic.
audience_target.demographics: Adults 18-44, slightly male-skewing on the hook but with strong female appeal through Ji-a and Joan; genre-literate streaming audience.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary New York locations, a modest cast, and moderate time-effect work keep this in indie feature territory rather than studio scale.

lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane where concept-forward genre meets character-first execution. The script has enough weirdness to feel fresh, but enough procedural clarity to be marketable to buyers who want a clean hook and a contained spend.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature with a contained central mystery and no clear sequel or spinoff vector beyond the lead's immediate case.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The cold open is a killer hook.
strengths.what_it_means: It gives the project immediate trailer value and a clean buyer-facing promise: this is not a standard procedural, it is a reality-bending murder mystery with a memorable first image. That kind of opening helps both packaging and audience positioning because it signals tone, stakes, and novelty in under five pages.
strengths.evidence: The empty Queens street, the driverless bus, and the old woman unloading an Uzi into Anthony before the scene resets.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Anthony is a playable lead role.
strengths.what_it_means: The script gives an actor a high-emotion, high-anxiety centerpiece that can carry a feature on internal tension alone. That makes the project attractive to talent looking for a showcase turn rather than a generic genre assignment.
strengths.evidence: Anthony’s panic attacks, his self-doubt about being a murderer, and the repeated moments where he tries to talk himself out of what he’s seeing.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Ji-a gives the movie a spine.
strengths.what_it_means: Her blunt competence turns the story from a one-man freakout into a two-track investigation with real procedural momentum. Buyers tend to respond to that because it broadens the audience entry point and gives the film a grounded counterweight to the surreal material.
strengths.evidence: Her evidence-board work, her no-nonsense interrogation style, and the rooftop moment where she becomes the only person who believes Anthony.

strengths.what_it_means: The repeated resets, disappearing evidence, and clock imagery create a visual grammar that can be marketed as a concept, not just explained as plot. That helps the film stand out in a crowded mystery-thriller field because the hook is legible in images.
strengths.evidence: The clock-shaped eye tattoo, the evidence locker erasing itself, and the rooftop sequence replaying with déjà vu.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The dialogue has a lived-in snap.
strengths.what_it_means: The banter between Anthony and Joan, and the friction between Ji-a and Larry, gives the script a voice that feels contemporary and castable. That kind of dialogue helps attract actors and directors who want genre material with personality rather than generic exposition.
strengths.evidence: Joan’s teasing, Ji-a’s “Time. Place. Fuck off.”, and the repeated name-misfires with Larry.

whats_special.headline: This is a clean, pitchable elevated-genre feature: a time-bending murder mystery with a strong cold open, a castable anxious lead, and a detective spine that keeps the story commercially legible. The contemporary New York footprint and modest cast keep it in indie territory, which makes the concept feel especially buyable for streamer originals, boutique financiers, or a director looking for a breakout first feature.

items.area: The time rules are still impressionistic.
items.detail: The script clearly wants the audience to feel the resets before it fully explains them, but the mechanics around what Anthony can change, what Ji-a remembers, and why evidence disappears are still loose on the page. That is a development-level friction point because the mystery depends on the audience trusting the logic even while the characters don’t.

items.area: The middle section leans on repetition.
items.detail: Several scenes circle the same emotional beat — Anthony panicking, Ji-a investigating, Joan deflecting, the clock motif reasserting itself — before the rooftop confrontation sharpens the stakes. A buyer will notice that the engine is strong, but the feature still needs a more forceful escalation pattern to feel fully propulsive.

items.area: Ji-a is compelling but still function-first.
items.detail: She has authority, attitude, and a clean investigative purpose, but the page mostly uses her as the audience’s procedural anchor rather than as a fully dimensional co-driver of the movie. That is not a deal-breaker, but it does narrow the emotional range of the film if the buyer is looking for a richer dual-protagonist dynamic.

items.area: XII arrives as mythology before character.
items.detail: The clock-eye tattoo, time-skipping, and ominous confidence make her memorable, but the scene is doing more world-building than humanizing. Producers will flag that as a useful hook with some risk: she is striking, but the script has not yet fully earned how much authority she has over the story.

issues.headline: The script’s biggest friction is not concept — it has that — but rule clarity and escalation. Buyers will respond to the hook immediately, then ask whether the time mechanics are precise enough and whether the middle can keep climbing with the same force as the cold open and rooftop reveal.
